Define once. Build many times.

FinKore is an open-source, language-agnostic specification that makes recurring financial behavior explicit, testable, and reusable across products and implementations. It defines how Money, Workflow, Audit, Approvals, and Financial Entities behave, how they fail, and what evidence they preserve.

The repository publishes the specification, portable acceptance cases, and an Agentic Contract for machine clients. You use these artifacts to build and evaluate an implementation in your own language and stack.

https://finkore.dev · Read the CoreDoc · Build an implementation

Why rebuild the same foundations?

CRUD is easy. Financial CRUD isn't.

An amount needs a currency, exact calculation, and explicit rounding. An approval needs to remain tied to the facts that justified it. A rejected workflow transition must preserve the state it was meant to change. An audit trail must retain enough evidence to explain what happened.

These questions recur across financial products, yet their answers often live inside application code, framework defaults, and decisions that are difficult to recover. Teams build, discover edge cases, fix, document, then repeat the work elsewhere.

FinKore brings those rules into a shared, inspectable contract. Your team can understand the expected behavior before writing code and check its results against portable acceptance cases afterward.

Your product may be unique. Your financial rules don't have to be.

FinKore is intended for engineers, architects, and financial-domain reviewers working on banks, fintechs, SaaS platforms, ERPs, and other financial systems. It provides a common reference for discussing behavior across teams and implementations.

FinKore makes explicitYour application decides
Observable values, results, errors, and invariantsLanguage, framework, API, storage, and deployment
How declared lifecycle and approval rules behaveBusiness policies, thresholds, permissions, and user experience
Stable requirements and portable acceptance casesWhich FinKore domains to implement and how to integrate them

This repository maintains the contract and its maintenance tools. Financial implementations, integrations, and conformance execution belong to consumers; there is no installable financial library, hosted service, or Conformance Runner here.

Ledger posting, tax, FX sourcing, reconciliation, settlement, and concrete accounting models remain outside the current Core scope. See the specification scope for the boundaries.

What the Core covers

Choose the domain that addresses the question in front of you:

DomainQuestions it answers
MoneyHow do amounts retain their currency and exact value through arithmetic, rounding, allocation, and serialization?
WorkflowWhich lifecycle changes are permitted, and what happens when a transition is rejected?
AuditWhat happened, who acted, and how is committed history preserved?
ApprovalsWhat was approved, under which conditions, and does that decision still apply?
Financial EntitiesHow does a financial subject retain its identity through validation, revisions, and permitted change?

Each domain defines observable behavior independently of implementation architecture. Together, they provide foundations your application can compose for its own financial use cases.

From financial principle to implementation

Start with the reason a rule exists, then follow it to its precise requirements and acceptance cases:

CoreDoc — financial principles and obligations
   ↓
Specification — precise behavior and stable requirement IDs
   ├── Conformance artifacts — portable inputs and expected observations
   └── Agentic Contract — canonical operation semantics for machine clients
                     ↓
       Consumer-owned implementations and integrations

CoreDoc states the foundation-level financial obligations. The specification refines them into requirements, invariants, and portable errors. Normative terms such as MUST, SHOULD, and MAY distinguish obligations, recommendations, and permissions; see the conventions for their meaning.

Conformance artifacts connect those requirements to portable acceptance cases, including failure, boundary, and mutation-sensitive cases. Stable IDs such as MONEY-ARITHMETIC-001 let you trace a rule to its supporting evidence. The manifest is the only entry point for discovering vector files.

The Agentic Contract describes canonical operations such as finkore.money.add: their inputs, outputs, errors, effects, and safety properties. Consumers provide executable integrations and authorization infrastructure. The specification remains authoritative for financial behavior.

You can begin with one domain. Read its rules, implement the selected scope, and use the published cases alongside your own evidence to evaluate the result. Consumers own invocation, observation, comparison, and reporting. Acceptance cases provide bounded evidence; their existence alone does not establish that an implementation conforms or that its behavior is exhaustively tested.

Contributing

Contributions start with a financial domain problem and CoreDoc alignment. Changes to behavior should connect specification requirements to conformance cases, traceability, and Agentic metadata where applicable. If the specification is silent, raise the gap before choosing new semantics.

See Contributing for the workflow and Contributor Licensing for the contribution terms. Published history is in the release notes.

Verify repository changes

The maintenance tools require Node >=24.11.0 <25. From the repository root, run:

npm ci --no-audit
npm run verify

After dependency installation, verification runs locally. It checks schemas, vector structure, requirement traceability, Agentic consistency, repository architecture, tool tests, documentation links, and licensing. These checks validate the published artifacts; consumers execute financial operations against their own implementations.

See Developer Tools for Node setup, individual checks, the separate npm run dependencies:audit review, and stable publication checks.
